fetched_contents.text: Human Subjects (RCR Role Plays) Role-Play Summary Resources on Responsibilities with Human Subjects Faculty Adviser Role Graduate Student Role Starting the Role Play Observer Role Role-Play Summary This role-play addresses issues involved with human subject research and working with an Institutional Review Board (IRB). The Belmont Report (1979) identifies three basic ethical principles that underlie all human subject research. These principles are Respect for persons, Beneficence, and Justice. Respect for persons requires us to treat individuals as autonomous human beings and not to use people as a means to an end. We must allow people to choose for themselves and provide extra protection to those with limited ability to choose, such as children. Rules derived from the principle of respect for persons include the requirements to obtain informed consent and to respect the privacy of research subjects. Beneficence reminds us to minimize harms and maximize benefits. Rules derived from the principle of beneficence include the requirement to use the best possible research design to maximize benefits and minimize harms, the requirement that researchers perform procedures competently and mitigate risks, and the prohibition of research whose risk-benefit ratio is unfavorable. Justice requires us to treat people fairly and to design research so that its burdens and benefits are shared equitably. Rules derived from the principle of justice include the requirement to select subjects equitably and the requirement to avoid exploitation of vulnerable populations or populations of convenience. IRBs ensure that research with human subjects follows these principles. Research may be reviewed by a convened Institutional Review Board (full review), by one or more IRB members (expedited review), or by an individual designated by the institution who may not be an IRB member (exemption approvals). Criteria for determining who will conduct the review include the level of risk, the type of research activity, vulnerability of subjects, and institution-specific criteria. It is a critical task to make the distinction between activities that meet the definition of research with human subjects and those that do not. If a project doesn’t meet the definition, it will not need review by an IRB. Consent forms are normally required except when the research involves no more than minimal risk or when subjects are anonymous. Informed consent begins with recruiting and screening of subjects and continues throughout the subjects’ involvement in the research procedures. Researchers must provide specific information about the study to subjects in a manner comprehensible to them, answer questions to better ensure subjects understand the research and their role in it, give subjects adequate time to consider their decisions, and obtain the voluntary agreement of subjects to participate in the study. The agreement is only to enter the study, because subjects may withdraw at any time, and they may decline to answer specific questions or complete specific tasks. This role-play also covered issues involving communication and collegiality. In this case, unfortunately, the data collected before IRB approval probably cannot be included in the analysis and publication. Structured role-playing can be a useful sociolinguistic elicitation method because it creates a controlled but realistic setting in which participants are prompted to use language in a socially meaningful way. The evidence points to role-play as a way to target pragmatic skills such as stylistic variation and requesting clarification, which are important sociolinguistic phenomena [N2-R1]. It can also be used in educational contexts to develop sociolinguistic competence by exposing learners to socially relevant interactional tasks [N2-R5]. In practice, role-play can be designed to elicit speech variables and interactional patterns that are difficult to observe in spontaneous settings, such as register shifts, dialectal variation, and institutional speech conventions [N2-R4].

A key advantage of role-playing is that it can expose register, dialect, and institutional language use by situating participants in scenarios that require them to adopt specific communicative identities or organizational roles. For example, the evidence notes that role-play can be used to reflect on “relationships and agendas” in a way that makes visible how language is shaped by social positioning [N1-R5]. It can also be used to study “identity construction in the speech of older adolescents and young adults learning French” [N2-R4], which is relevant to dialect and register because identity is often expressed through linguistic choice. In organizational contexts, role-play can help observe how language is adapted to bureaucratic roles and scenarios, such as management team roles or public administration tasks [N5-R2][N5-R4]. These scenarios are especially informative for sociolinguistic study because they require participants to perform language in ways that are institutionally sanctioned, normative, or role-specific [N5-R2].

Despite these strengths, role-play is a limited proxy for spontaneous language behavior. The evidence does not explicitly describe a large body of direct empirical results on spontaneous vs. role-played behavior, but the methodological logic is clear: role-play is an elicitation task, not an unstructured naturalistic observation. That means participants may not speak in the same way they would in a genuine interaction, and their behavior may be influenced by the task, the role, and the researcher’s framing rather than by spontaneous social motivation [N2-R5]. The practical implication is that role-play data should be treated as contextualized performance rather than as a direct measure of everyday language use [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Overall, structured role-playing is well suited to revealing sociolinguistic phenomena such as pragmatic variation, identity construction, register, dialect, and institutional language use [N1-R5][N2-R1][N2-R4]. Its major limitation is that it is an elicited rather than spontaneous behavior, which may reduce ecological validity and obscure the full complexity of authentic language in use [N2-R5].

### Bottom line

Structured role-playing games can gather sociolinguistic data in bureaucratic settings because they elicit language in a controlled but socially meaningful way, exposing register, dialect, and institutional language use while also allowing researchers to study interactional patterns and pragmatic variation [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
